newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Court stops call for execution of British nurses.
newsitem.headline: Court stops call for execution of British nurses.

text.p: An Australian court on Friday temporarily barred the brother of murdered Australian nurse Yvonne Gilford from calling for the death penalty for two British nurses charged with killing her in Saudi Arabia.
The South Australian state supreme court ordered Frank Gilford not to make further comments on behalf of his family until his mother's mental state had been assessed.
Under Saudi law, a call for the death penalty by a victim's family must be unanimous, lawyers representing the British nurses told the court.
The lawyers said Yvonne's mother, Muriel Gilford, who suffers from Alzheimer's disease, is not mentally competent to agree with her son's call for execution.
Judge Len King issued a temporary restraining order against Frank Gilford pending a study of his mother's mental state.

"Until further orders the defendant (Frank Gilford) be restrained...from further advising the Saudi Arabian court that it is the unanimous view of the heirs that the death penalty be inflicted...," King said in his judgment.
King ordered Frank Gilford to notify the Saudi court of his ruling and that Muriel Gilford's health documents be made available to the British nurses' lawyers.

Yvonne Gilford, 51, was found murdered in her dormitory room at the King Fahd medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dhahran on December 11 last year, having been stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated.
British nurses Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLaughlan, 31, have been charged with murdering Gilford, but have said they are innocent, despite initially signing confessions.
If found guilty the nurses face the death penalty, which in Saudi Arabia is traditionally a public beheading by the sword.
According to Islamic sharia law the victim's family may demand the death penalty if the court finds the women guilty and says capital punishment is appropriate.

Sources close to the case told Reuters last month the Kohbar sharia court which is hearing the trial had questioned the power of attorney which Gilford's mother had given her son but had granted him the right to demand execution if the nurses were found guilty.

However the defendants' Saudi law firm, Salah al-Hujailan, later said the court, which is due to resume on August 10, was leaning towards disqualifying the Gilford family from any role in the nurses' fate.
